title: A minimal model for the Weyl nodes and Fermi arcs of PtBi$_2$
authors: Tobias Cristófoli, Manuel Alonso Lemos, Jorge I. Facio, Pablo S. Cornaglia
abstract: Weyl semimetals host topologically protected Fermi arcs on their surfaces, originating from the Chern number of the bulk Weyl nodes. In trigonal PtBi$_2$, superconducting signatures have been associated with the Fermi arcs. Theoretical descriptions of this surface superconductivity have so far relied on effective models that are not directly tied to the microscopic electronic structure of the material. In this work we develop a minimal description of the low-energy bands guided by density functional theory calculations and fully constrained by the relevant crystalline and time-reversal symmetries. The model captures the evolution of the Weyl nodes with spin-orbit coupling, including node annihilations, and is able to describe the spin-momentum locking of the surface Fermi arcs. It reproduces the orbital content and the band topology of PtBi$_2$ and provides a starting point for further studies.
summary: This theoretical work develops a minimal, symmetry-constrained model for describing Weyl nodes and Fermi arcs in the topological semimetal $	ext{PtBi}_2$. By incorporating spin-orbit coupling terms derived from DFT, the authors successfully predict how these nodes split and annihilate. The resulting Hamiltonian provides a robust starting point for understanding surface superconductivity mechanisms in such materials.
main_problem: The work aims to develop a minimal, symmetry-constrained theoretical model for understanding the topological electronic features—Weyl nodes and Fermi arcs—in the Weyl semimetal $	ext{PtBi}_2$. This bridges the gap between complex *ab initio* calculations and simplified effective descriptions.
main_result: A minimal Hamiltonian was constructed that successfully reproduces the topology, captures the spin-orbit coupling (SOC)-driven splitting, and models the subsequent annihilation of Weyl nodes in momentum space. The model also describes the characteristic spin-momentum locking on surface Fermi arcs.
method: The methodology combines symmetry analysis (using tools like qsymm) with continuum Hamiltonian construction, guided by DFT results to constrain low-energy band physics.
model_or_system: The system is trigonal $	ext{PtBi}_2$, modeled using a tight-binding approach incorporating orbital degrees of freedom ($\{p_x, p_y\}$) and SOC terms. The Hamiltonian is built sector-by-sector to enforce crystal symmetries ($C_{3v}$) across multiple coupled blocks.
key_observables: Weyl node chirality ($\chi$), Fermi arc spin texture (spin polarization $\langle S_z angle/ho$), and the evolution of nodes/arcs as a function of SOC coupling strength ($\lambda$).
important_parameters: SOC couplings ($g_1, g_2$, etc.), critical coupling strengths ($g_c$) for node annihilation, and momentum-dependent terms derived from DFT.
main_assumptions: The model assumes that the low-energy physics is dominated by specific orbital components ($	ext{Bi } 6p$ orbitals) and that the Hamiltonian can be effectively described by a minimal set of symmetry-allowed terms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate band structures near Weyl nodes, map the twelve Weyl points in the Brillouin zone under $C_{3v}$ symmetry, and show the evolution of node trajectories as SOC strength increases. Surface density of states plots confirm the presence and spin texture of Fermi arcs.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing a basic model constrained by symmetries to incorporating SOC terms that cause node splitting and annihilation. It then extends this description to incorporate full $C_{3v}$ symmetry via multi-sector coupling, culminating in a detailed analysis of how different SOC components affect spin texture and nodal structure.
why_interesting: While focused on topological materials physics rather than AMO systems, the rigorous use of symmetry constraints to build an effective Hamiltonian from first principles is highly relevant. The techniques for analyzing band topology and emergent symmetries are transferable to understanding exotic phases in quantum simulators or superconducting qubits.
